clips.text: In the winter of 32/31 BC, Antony sails back to the Peloponnese and winters at Patrae.
clips.spoken: In the winter of 32/31 BC, Antony sails back to the Peloponnese and winters at PAT-ree.

clips.text: He spreads his soldiers to guard the strategic points and secure provisions.
clips.spoken: He spreads his soldiers to guard the strategic points and secure provisions.

clips.text: His garrisons hold Corcyra, and he holds Methone.
clips.spoken: His garrisons hold kor-SY-ruh, and he holds meh-THOH-nee.

clips.text: We have drawn this chain of posts as guarding the supply route from Egypt. That is our reading, not the sources' words.
clips.spoken: We have drawn this chain of posts as guarding the supply route from Egypt. That is our reading, not the sources' words.

clips.text: Then the other side moves.
clips.spoken: Then the other side moves.

clips.text: Before spring 31 BC, Agrippa takes Methone by storm, and kills Bogud there.
clips.spoken: Before spring 31 BC, Agrippa takes meh-THOH-nee by storm, and kills BOH-gud there.

clips.text: From there he watches for the merchant ships, and raids the coasts of Greece.
clips.spoken: From there he watches for the merchant ships, and raids the coasts of Greece.

clips.text: Those merchant ships were probably grain ships from Egypt, though that is our reading, not the source's.
clips.spoken: Those merchant ships were probably grain ships from Egypt, though that is our reading, not the source's.

clips.text: In spring 31 BC, Octavian crosses the Ionian Gulf from Brundisium with his whole force.
clips.spoken: In spring 31 BC, Octavian crosses the Ionian Gulf from Brundisium with his whole force.

clips.text: His cavalry lands at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains.
clips.spoken: His cavalry lands at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains.

clips.text: He seizes Corcyra, abandoned by its garrisons, and occupies Toryne in Epirus.
clips.spoken: He seizes kor-SY-ruh, abandoned by its garrisons, and occupies TOR-ih-nee in Epirus.

clips.text: He camps on the high ground north of the strait, where Nicopolis later stood.
clips.spoken: He camps on the high ground north of the strait, where Nicopolis later stood.

clips.text: From Toryne he probably marched south to that camp; the sources give the places, not the road.
clips.spoken: From TOR-ih-nee he probably marched south to that camp; the sources give the places, not the road.

clips.text: In summer 31 BC, Agrippa takes Leucas, then Patrae after beating Nasidius at sea, and later Corinth.
clips.spoken: In summer 31 BC, Agrippa takes LOO-kus, then PAT-ree after beating nuh-SID-ee-us at sea, and later Corinth.

clips.text: Antony's forces lose men to disease and desertion.
clips.spoken: Antony's forces lose men to disease and desertion.

clips.text: Cut off from bringing in grain, his provisions begin to fail.
clips.spoken: Cut off from bringing in grain, his provisions begin to fail.

clips.text: Now to the battle itself.
clips.spoken: Now to the battle itself.

clips.text: The battle is fought on 2 September, 31 BC.
clips.spoken: The battle is fought on 2 September, 31 BC.

clips.text: That morning, Antony's fleet draws up its line a little outside the strait, and comes no further. He has ordered his ships to hold their position at the narrow mouth of the gulf.
clips.spoken: That morning, Antony's fleet draws up its line a little outside the strait, and comes no further. He has ordered his ships to hold their position at the narrow mouth of the gulf.

clips.text: Octavian keeps his ships about eight furlongs away, some 1.5 kilometres, and waits a long time.
clips.spoken: Octavian keeps his ships about eight furlongs away, some 1.5 kilometres, and waits a long time.

clips.text: Cleopatra's sixty ships lie behind the line.
clips.spoken: Cleopatra's sixty ships lie behind the line.

clips.text: Who commanded where? The sources disagree. Plutarch puts Antony on his own right wing with Publicola, Marcus Octavius and Marcus Insteius in the centre, and Coelius on the left. Against them, Agrippa holds Octavian's left, and Octavian keeps the right for himself.
clips.spoken: Who commanded where? The sources disagree. Plutarch puts Antony on his own right wing with pub-LIK-oh-luh, Marcus Octavius and Marcus in-STAY-us in the centre, and SEE-lee-us on the left. Against them, Agrippa holds Octavian's left, and Octavian keeps the right for himself.

clips.text: Velleius gives Antony's fleet to Publicola and Sosius. On Octavian's side, he puts Lurius on the right, Arruntius on the left, and Agrippa in charge of the whole fight at sea.
clips.spoken: Velleius gives Antony's fleet to pub-LIK-oh-luh and SOH-shee-us. On Octavian's side, he puts LOO-ree-us on the right, uh-RUN-shus on the left, and Agrippa in charge of the whole fight at sea.

clips.text: A modern summary, on Wikipedia, combines the two: it gives Octavian's centre to Arruntius, and Antony's left wing to Sosius, which neither ancient passage we hold does.
clips.spoken: A modern summary, on Wikipedia, combines the two: it gives Octavian's centre to uh-RUN-shus, and Antony's left wing to SOH-shee-us, which neither ancient passage we hold does.

clips.text: The map draws just one arrangement, as a reconstruction. It does not settle the question.
clips.spoken: The map draws just one arrangement, as a reconstruction. It does not settle the question.

clips.text: Plutarch tells us that at the sixth hour, about midday, with a wind rising from the sea, Antony's men put their left wing in motion.
clips.spoken: Plutarch tells us that at the sixth hour, about midday, with a wind rising from the sea, Antony's men put their left wing in motion.

clips.text: Octavian orders his right wing to row backwards, to draw them out of the gulf and the narrows.
clips.spoken: Octavian orders his right wing to row backwards, to draw them out of the gulf and the narrows.

clips.text: Into the afternoon, Agrippa extends his wing to encircle them. Publicola advances against him, and is cut off from the centre.
clips.spoken: Into the afternoon, Agrippa extends his wing to encircle them. pub-LIK-oh-luh advances against him, and is cut off from the centre.

clips.text: Antony's centre falls into confusion, engaging Arruntius.
clips.spoken: Antony's centre falls into confusion, engaging uh-RUN-shus.

clips.text: We have placed this on the northern side of the battle; the compass point is our reading, not the sources'.
clips.spoken: We have placed this on the northern side of the battle; the compass point is our reading, not the sources'.

clips.text: Then, in Plutarch's words, "suddenly the sixty ships of Cleopatra were seen hoisting their sails for flight and making off through the midst of the combatants."
clips.spoken: Then, in Plutarch's words, "suddenly the sixty ships of Cleopatra were seen hoisting their sails for flight and making off through the midst of the combatants."

clips.text: They take advantage of the wind, and make for the Peloponnese.
clips.spoken: They take advantage of the wind, and make for the Peloponnese.

clips.text: Dio says she turned to flight from the strain of waiting, and signalled her ships.
clips.spoken: Dio says she turned to flight from the strain of waiting, and signalled her ships.

clips.text: Velleius puts it on her: Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight, and Antony chose to go with her rather than stay with his fighting men.
clips.spoken: Velleius puts it on her: Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight, and Antony chose to go with her rather than stay with his fighting men.

clips.text: Panic, her initiative, or a planned breakout? Did Cleopatra, and perhaps Antony too, plan the flight before the battle began? Did her squadron escape through a gap in the line? These questions are still open.
clips.spoken: Panic, her initiative, or a planned breakout? Did Cleopatra, and perhaps Antony too, plan the flight before the battle began? Did her squadron escape through a gap in the line? These questions are still open.

clips.text: Antony leaves the fight in a five-oared galley, with only Alexas the Syrian and Scellius beside him, and goes after her.
clips.spoken: Antony leaves the fight in a five-oared galley, with only Alexas the Syrian and SKEL-ee-us beside him, and goes after her.

clips.text: Dio says he thought her ships fled from fear, not at her bidding, and so he followed.
clips.spoken: Dio says he thought her ships fled from fear, not at her bidding, and so he followed.

clips.text: We have drawn from this that the fleet left behind has probably lost its commander.
clips.spoken: We have drawn from this that the fleet left behind has probably lost its commander.

clips.text: But not its money. Dio says the money was still aboard the ships left fighting, and Octavian held back from fire to gain it.
clips.spoken: But not its money. Dio says the money was still aboard the ships left fighting, and Octavian held back from fire to gain it.

clips.text: Was this desertion, or a planned escape? Historians still disagree.
clips.spoken: Was this desertion, or a planned escape? Historians still disagree.

clips.text: Late in the afternoon, with the fight still even, Octavian sends to the camp for fire.
clips.spoken: Late in the afternoon, with the fight still even, Octavian sends to the camp for fire.

clips.text: His ships attack from many sides, with blazing missiles, torches, and pots of charcoal and pitch.
clips.spoken: His ships attack from many sides, with blazing missiles, torches, and pots of charcoal and pitch.

clips.text: Plutarch says Antony's fleet held out until the tenth hour, worn down by a rising sea, and that three hundred ships were captured, "as Caesar himself has written."
clips.spoken: Plutarch says Antony's fleet held out until the tenth hour, worn down by a rising sea, and that three hundred ships were captured, "as Caesar himself has written."

clips.text: On land, Antony's legions hold together for seven days, ignoring Octavian's messages.
clips.spoken: On land, Antony's legions hold together for seven days, ignoring Octavian's messages.

clips.text: Then Canidius, their general, runs away by night, and the army goes over to Octavian without fighting.
clips.spoken: Then kuh-NID-ee-us, their general, runs away by night, and the army goes over to Octavian without fighting.

clips.text: After the battle, the story leaves Actium behind.
clips.spoken: After the battle, the story leaves AK-tee-um behind.

clips.text: Antony is taken aboard Cleopatra's ship. He means to cross from Taenarum to Libya.
clips.spoken: Antony is taken aboard Cleopatra's ship. He means to cross from TEE-nuh-rum to Libya.

clips.text: Where she parted from him, the sources differ. Dio says they went as far as the Peloponnese together, and from there Cleopatra hastened to Egypt. Plutarch has her go with him to Libya, and on into Egypt from Paraetonium.
clips.spoken: Where she parted from him, the sources differ. Dio says they went as far as the Peloponnese together, and from there Cleopatra hastened to Egypt. Plutarch has her go with him to Libya, and on into Egypt from pa-ree-TOH-nee-um.

clips.text: Dio says Antony sailed to Pinarius Scarpus and the army kept in Africa for the protection of Egypt. Scarpus refused to receive him, and killed the men Antony sent ahead.
clips.spoken: Dio says Antony sailed to Pinarius Scarpus and the army kept in Africa for the protection of Egypt. Scarpus refused to receive him, and killed the men Antony sent ahead.

clips.text: Plutarch says that when the general holding his forces in Libya brought about their defection, Antony tried to kill himself, and his friends took him to Alexandria.
clips.spoken: Plutarch says that when the general holding his forces in Libya brought about their defection, Antony tried to kill himself, and his friends took him to Alexandria.

clips.text: Plutarch's general is unnamed; most likely he was Scarpus.
clips.spoken: Plutarch's general is unnamed; most likely he was Scarpus.

clips.text: Antony is at Paraetonium until the news of Pelusium.
clips.spoken: Antony is at pa-ree-TOH-nee-um until the news of peh-LOO-zee-um.

clips.text: Cornelius Gallus takes over Scarpus' army, marches suddenly on Paraetonium, and occupies it.
clips.spoken: Cornelius Gallus takes over Scarpus' army, marches suddenly on pa-ree-TOH-nee-um, and occupies it.

clips.text: Before Alexandria, Antony's fleet goes over to Octavian. Plutarch tells it as the crews' own choice; Dio has Cleopatra cause the ships to desert.
clips.spoken: Before Alexandria, Antony's fleet goes over to Octavian. Plutarch tells it as the crews' own choice; Dio has Cleopatra cause the ships to desert.

clips.text: His cavalry deserts, his infantry is beaten, and he retires into the city.
clips.spoken: His cavalry deserts, his infantry is beaten, and he retires into the city.

clips.text: Told that Cleopatra is dead, Antony wounds himself, and dies with her in the tomb.
clips.spoken: Told that Cleopatra is dead, Antony wounds himself, and dies with her in the tomb.

clips.text: Octavian drives into the city.
clips.spoken: Octavian drives into the city.

clips.text: The city fell, by the usual account, on 1 August 30 BC; no passage we hold gives the date.
clips.spoken: The city fell, by the usual account, on 1 August 30 BC; no passage we hold gives the date.

clips.text: Cleopatra dies. Octavian admires her spirit, and has her buried with Antony.
clips.spoken: Cleopatra dies. Octavian admires her spirit, and has her buried with Antony.

clips.text: Octavian now holds all power alone. Dio dates that from Actium, not from Alexandria.
clips.spoken: Octavian now holds all power alone. Dio dates that from AK-tee-um, not from Alexandria.
